prompt:
You are advising Niveo, a nine-person startup building software for pediatric oncology infusion centers. Its prototype reads medication orders, current weight, lab values, and pump settings, then warns when they do not match the chemotherapy protocol. Today is July 14, 2026. The team must choose what to do through October 31 before eleven months of runway becomes seven.

In 18 interviews, 13 pharmacy or nursing leaders asked for an "autopause" that would stop an infusion when the model flags a mismatch; six asked to buy it as an add-on to the pump. Two institutions sent letters calling the idea urgent. Yet in six days of shadowing across two centers, nurses overrode 31 of 36 existing pump alerts, most often because the pump lacked a same-day weight, renal adjustment, or physician-approved exception. For 22 of those overrides they called a pharmacist or physician before continuing. Niveo's retrospective model correctly flagged nine of ten known order discrepancies but also raised 47 extra alerts in 600 infusions. No clinician has used it in live care. One center allowed deidentified record review, but neither has approved an EHR or pump integration.

A children's hospital innovation director says an unpaid eight-week pilot can begin in September if autopause is ready, but pharmacy, bedside nursing, safety, IT security, and procurement have not named owners or signed off. Another hospital's CFO said "$180,000 per site sounds reasonable if you prevent a serious error," while its clinical lead has not shared data. The accelerator partner wants a 20-hospital waitlist and a price page before Demo Day. Engineering estimates it can ship autopause in three weeks, and the CTO argues that any delay will kill the pilot.

A serious dosing error is rare but potentially catastrophic. A chemotherapy cycle is typically 21 to 42 days, delayed toxicity can appear after discharge, and installation, security, and procurement can take months. The medical adviser says automatic interruption is not ethically ready for patient care under the current approvals. The founders are also being invited to adapt the model for adult infusion clinics and veterinary oncology; those buyers appear easier to reach, but the team has no observed workflow in either market.

Write the founders a decision memo for what the company should do next.
criteria: The memo explicitly treats the autopause requests, urgency letters, and CFO price comment as weaker evidence than observed behavior; it uses the 31-of-36 overrides and 22 escalation calls to state one falsifiable actor-workflow-consequence explanation, at least two plausible alternative explanations, and one observation that would disconfirm the preferred explanation.

The memo names one narrow pediatric-oncology participant/workflow cohort, gives a rationale beyond convenient access, and specifies an inclusion rule, an exclusion rule, a recruitment owner, and consent or data-access handling.

The memo keeps patient-facing automatic interruption out of the next test and separately addresses model performance, clinical workflow fit, and patient safety through a bounded sandbox or silent-mode evaluation with independent clinical or safety review, monitoring, rollback or fallback, and follow-up spanning at least one 21-to-42-day treatment cycle.

The memo defines at least one numeric evidence threshold, at least one assumed calendar review date, and an explicit stop rule, then states distinct next actions for a passed, failed, and inconclusive result without claiming that retrospective accuracy, letters, a waitlist, an unpaid pilot, or a hypothetical price validates demand.

The memo does not launch broad acquisition, commit the autopause specification to shipping, set pricing from the CFO quote, or enter adult or veterinary oncology now; it permits growth only to recruit the defined sample, tests willingness to pay through a concrete commitment tied to workflow access or deployment and procurement, and assigns downstream ownership for validated build, validated growth, pricing design, and unresolved expansion.
